title: Variables and Data Types
summary: Store values in typed variables: int, long, double, boolean, char, and String, plus constants and var.
intro: Programs need to remember things: a score, a name, a price. In Java you store each value in a variable, and every variable has a type that the compiler checks before your program runs.

steps.title: Declaring variables

example.title: Player profile
example.prompt: Declare a player's name, level, health, and online flag, print each on a labeled line, then raise the level and print its line again.
example.output:
Name: Nova
Level: 7
Health: 87.5
Online: true
Level: 8
example.explanation: Each declaration names a type, a variable, and a starting value. Every labeled line is two calls: `print` writes the label and stays on the line, then `println` writes the value and ends it. `level = 8;` has no type because `level` already exists, so the last line shows the new value.

practice.title: Book listing
practice.prompt:
Describe a book with four variables, then change its price.

1. Declare `title` as the String `"Dune"`, `pages` as the int `412`, `price` as the double `18.99`, and `inStock` as the boolean `true`.
2. Print each one on a labeled line, in that order, with the labels `Title: `, `Pages: `, `Price: `, and `In stock: `.
3. Set `price` to `20.0` and print the `Price: ` line again.

Expected output:

```text
Title: Dune
Pages: 412
Price: 18.99
In stock: true
Price: 20.0
```

tests.output:
Title: Dune
Pages: 412
Price: 18.99
In stock: true
Price: 20.0

hints: Copy the shape of the example: four declarations, four print and println pairs, one reassignment, one more pair.
`price` already exists, so reassign it without writing its type again.
A whole double still prints its decimal point, so the last line is `Price: 20.0`.

steps.title: More primitive types
steps.body:
Java has eight primitive types:

| Type | Holds | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `byte` | -128 to 127 | `byte b = 100;` |
| `short` | -32,768 to 32,767 | `short s = 2026;` |
| `int` | about -2.1 to 2.1 billion | `int n = 42;` |
| `long` | about -9.2 to 9.2 quintillion | `long big = 5_000_000_000L;` |
| `float` | decimal, about 7 digits | `float f = 1.5f;` |
| `double` | decimal, about 15 digits | `double d = 1.5;` |
| `char` | one character | `char c = 'Z';` |
| `boolean` | `true` or `false` | `boolean ok = false;` |

A `char` uses single quotes: `'Z'` is a char, `"Z"` is a String.

A whole-number literal is an `int` unless it ends in `L`, so `long big = 5000000000;` fails with the error *integer number too large*. Add the `L`, and write it uppercase because a lowercase `l` looks like `1`. A decimal literal is a `double`, so a `float` needs `f`: `float f = 1.5;` does not compile.

Underscores make numbers readable: `1_000_000` is just `1000000` and prints without them. A value outside a type's range, like `byte b = 200;`, is a compile error. Prefer `double` over `float` unless you have a reason.

example.title: Big and small numbers
example.prompt: Store a grade letter, the world population as a long, a float temperature, and one million written with underscores, then print each on a labeled line.
example.output:
Grade: A
World population: 8100000000
Temperature: 21.5
One million: 1000000
example.explanation: `'A'` is a char because of the single quotes. The population needs `long` and the `L` suffix because 8.1 billion is past the int limit. `21.5f` is a float literal, and without the `f` it would be a double. The underscores in the source are only for your eyes, so the printed numbers have none.

practice.title: Mixed types
practice.prompt:
Store four values of different primitive types and print each on a labeled line.

1. Declare `initial` as the char `'J'`.
2. Declare `msPerYear` as a long holding `31_536_000_000L`, the milliseconds in a 365-day year.
3. Declare `ratio` as the float `0.75f` and `volume` as the byte `42`.
4. Print them in that order with the labels `Initial: `, `Milliseconds per year: `, `Ratio: `, and `Volume: `.

Expected output:

```text
Initial: J
Milliseconds per year: 31536000000
Ratio: 0.75
Volume: 42
```

tests.output:
Initial: J
Milliseconds per year: 31536000000
Ratio: 0.75
Volume: 42

hints: Follow the example: one declaration per value, then a print and println pair for each.
The long literal needs its `L` and the float needs its `f`, or the code will not compile.
A byte holds -128 to 127, so `42` fits and needs no suffix.

steps.title: Constants and var

example.title: Game settings
example.prompt: Declare two constants above main, a final local, and two var locals, then print all five on labeled lines.
example.output:
Max players: 4
Tax rate: 0.08
Max score: 100
City: Lisbon
Count: 12
example.explanation: `MAX_PLAYERS` and `TAX_RATE` live in `Main` above `main`, and `static` lets `main` read them. `maxScore` is final, so any later assignment to it would not compile. Java infers String for `city` and int for `count` from their values, so they print like any other variable.

practice.title: Course settings
practice.prompt:
Declare two constants, a final local, and two var locals, then print all five.

1. Above `main`, declare `static final` constants `DAYS_PER_WEEK` as the int `7` and `PI_APPROX` as the double `3.14`.
2. Inside `main`, declare a final int local `passMark` holding `60`.
3. Declare `username` as `"coder42"` and `age` as `19`, both with `var`.
4. Print all five in that order with the labels `Days per week: `, `Pi approx: `, `Pass mark: `, `Username: `, and `Age: `.

Expected output:

```text
Days per week: 7
Pi approx: 3.14
Pass mark: 60
Username: coder42
Age: 19
```

tests.output:
Days per week: 7
Pi approx: 3.14
Pass mark: 60
Username: coder42
Age: 19

hints: Constants go inside the class braces but outside `main`, and each one starts with `static final` followed by its type.
`var` takes the place of the type name. The rest of the declaration stays the same.
Print the constants by name, exactly like any other variable.

recap:
- Declare with `type name = value;`, and reassign with `name = value;` (no type).
- Java has eight primitives: `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`. `String` is a class.
- A whole double prints with `.0`, like `20.0`.
- Whole-number literals are `int` unless they end in `L`. Float literals need `f`.
- `byte` holds -128 to 127 and `short` holds -32,768 to 32,767.
- `1_000_000` is just a readable `1000000`.
- `static final` constants go above `main` in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. A `final` variable cannot be reassigned.
- `var` infers a local's type from its initializer, works only for locals, and `var x = 20;` is an `int`.
